explanations.explanation: The father says it himself: “A spirit keeps seizing him, and he screams abruptly.” He goes on to say it throws the boy into convulsions so that he foams at the mouth. That's a dad who describes exactly what he's seen, no sugarcoating. Hold onto that, because it sets up everything Jesus does next.

explanations.answer: A fever will not leave him
explanations.explanation: No fever shows up anywhere in this man's words. What he describes is a spirit that keeps seizing his son, with screaming, convulsions and foaming at the mouth. Fevers are a whole different problem than what he lays out here. Stick with the spirit, because that's what Jesus ends up dealing with.

explanations.answer: He has been blind from birth
explanations.explanation: Blindness never comes up in this passage. The father talks about a spirit that keeps seizing his son and throws him into convulsions. Nothing about the boy's eyes at all. His whole plea is about that spirit and how rarely it leaves the boy alone.

The father tells Jesus, “I begged Your disciples to drive it out, but they were unable.” He doesn't dress it up or soften it. He just reports what happened, straight to Jesus' face. Honest to the bone, that man.
Priests never come into this scene. The father says he begged Jesus' disciples to drive the spirit out. And then he says they were unable. Then he cries out to Jesus in front of the crowd.
The elders aren't mentioned here. This dad says he went to Jesus' disciples and begged them to drive it out. They were unable. So he brings the problem to Jesus Himself.
After His “How long must I remain with you…” line, Jesus tells the father, “Bring your son here.” No speech about it. Jesus calls the boy to Himself. Short and clear, and the father has his answer.

explanations.answer: Go home and he will be well
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't send the father home. He says, “Bring your son here.” The boy is going to be brought to Him. Jesus wants to deal with this face to face.

explanations.answer: Wait for Me in the town
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't tell anyone to wait in a town. He says, “Bring your son here.” The father and the boy are meeting Jesus right where the crowd is. Not a single word about moving the scene somewhere else.

explanations.answer: Rebukes the spirit and heals the boy
explanations.explanation: Even after the boy is slammed to the ground, Jesus rebukes the unclean spirit and heals the boy. Jesus does it Himself, right there. The spirit slammed him down, and Jesus still wasn't done. I think the dad needed to see exactly that.

explanations.answer: Tells His disciples to try again
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets sent back for a second attempt here. The text says Jesus Himself rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy. The disciples had already been unable, as the father said. Jesus steps in and handles it personally.

explanations.answer: Sends the boy to see the priest
explanations.explanation: No priest is in this scene, and nobody gets sent anywhere. Jesus rebukes the unclean spirit, heals the boy and gives him back to his father. All of it happens right there in front of the crowd. The boy never has to leave to get help.

Luke says Jesus healed the boy “…and gave him back to his father.” Think about who that father is: a man who called this boy his only child. I think this is the line to sit with for a second. The boy is well, and Jesus gives him back to his dad.

The text says the opposite of false. Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and “…gave him back to his father.” The father who begged for his only child gets him back. That's what Luke tells us.

They don't catch it. Luke says, “But they did not understand this statement.” It was veiled from them so that they could not comprehend it. So the disciples hear Jesus say it and still can't make sense of it.

That's right, they don't understand it. Luke says, “But they did not understand this statement.” It was veiled from them so they could not comprehend it. And they were afraid to ask Jesus about it, so the confusion just sat there.

explanations.answer: Which of them would be the greatest
explanations.explanation: Luke says an argument started among the disciples “…as to which of them would be the greatest.” Jesus had just told them something heavy about the Son of Man. And the next thing you know, they're comparing rankings. I'd like to say I've never seen that kind of thing, but I'd be lying.

explanations.answer: Which of them should carry the money
explanations.explanation: Money isn't what they're arguing about. The text says the argument was about which of them would be the greatest. It's about rank, not a wallet. Luke doesn't mention money anywhere in this scene.

explanations.answer: Which town they should go to next
explanations.explanation: No travel plans here. Luke says the argument was about which of them would be the greatest. The text doesn't mention a next town at all. It's all about who's on top.

Jesus, knowing the thoughts of their hearts, “…had a little child stand beside Him.” He doesn't start with a lecture. He sets a child right there where everyone can see. Then He speaks to them about welcoming that child in His name.

No soldier shows up in this scene. Jesus knows the thoughts of their hearts and has a little child stand beside Him. That's who He brings into the middle of the argument. A child, standing right at His side.
A tax collector isn't in this scene. Jesus has a little child stand beside Him. That's who He brings in when the argument has started among the disciples. And that child is the picture He uses next.

Jesus says, “Whoever welcomes this little child in My name welcomes Me…” Then He adds, “…and whoever welcomes Me welcomes the One who sent Me.” So welcoming that child in His name connects straight to Him. That's a big deal for a little child standing right beside Him.
Jesus doesn't say a prophet here. He says, “Whoever welcomes this little child in My name welcomes Me…” The line points straight to Himself. And then past Himself to the One who sent Him.

An angel isn't in Jesus' words here. He says, “Whoever welcomes this little child in My name welcomes Me…” He's talking about Himself, and then about the One who sent Him. The child in front of them is the picture.

Jesus says, “For whoever is the least among all of you, he is the greatest.” That flips the whole argument over. They were fighting over who ranks first, and He answers with the least. I picture some very quiet disciples after that one.

Jesus really does say it. His words are, “For whoever is the least among all of you, he is the greatest.” That's His answer to an argument about who's greatest. So this one is true, straight from the text.

John, one of Jesus' disciples, says, “we saw someone driving out demons in Your name…” The man was doing it in Jesus' name, and John says that right up front. So the disciples spotted a man doing the very thing they had struggled with earlier. And John goes on to say what they did about it.
John, one of Jesus' disciples, doesn't mention healing the blind. He says they saw someone driving out demons in Jesus' name. Then he says they tried to stop him. Healing the blind never comes up.

Teaching in a synagogue isn't what John, one of Jesus' disciples, describes. He says they saw someone driving out demons in Jesus' name. That's the action he reports to Jesus. Nothing about a synagogue at all.

explanations.answer: He was not traveling with them
explanations.explanation: John gives the reason himself: “…we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us.” The man was driving out demons in Jesus' name, and the problem was that he wasn't with their group. That's the whole complaint. Jesus answers it in the very next verse.
Money isn't John's complaint. He says they tried to stop the man “…because he does not accompany us.” That's the reason John gives. The text says nothing about payment.

explanations.answer: He was one of the Pharisees
explanations.explanation: John never says the man was a Pharisee. His reason is that the man “…does not accompany us.” That's the reason he gives. The man simply wasn't traveling with them.

Jesus says, “Do not stop him, for whoever is not against you is for you.” The word is “against,” and it's a short one. The man was driving out demons in Jesus' name. So Jesus tells the disciples to leave him alone.

Close, but that's not Jesus' word. He says, “…whoever is not against you is for you.” John said the man does not accompany them, and Jesus still says not to stop him. The word Jesus uses is “against.”
That isn't the word Jesus uses. His line is, “…whoever is not against you is for you.” Nothing here is about who's ahead and who's behind. It's about whether someone is against you or not.
